# Decisions

Architecture and design decisions that shaped the site, with the reasoning that made
them. Superseding a decision means adding a new entry, not editing the old one.

---

## D-01 — Static multi-page site, generated from templates

**Decision:** The deliverable is plain HTML with no framework, generated by a small
Python build.

**Why:** A marketing site has no state to manage. A framework would add a build chain,
a dependency surface and a deploy artefact without buying anything. Generating from
fragments keeps the header, footer and CTA identical across 19 pages while leaving the
output deployable as files.

**Cost:** A build step before publishing, and a generator to maintain.

---

## D-02 — Everything inlined: CSS, JS, fonts

**Decision:** Each page carries its own CSS, JavaScript and both typefaces as base64.

**Why:** The site must render identically from a folder, from a static host, and inside
the review environment, with no network. Embedded fonts also eliminate the flash of
fallback text that makes a premium page feel cheap on first load.

**Cost:** Each page is ~150 KB, and shared assets are duplicated. Acceptable for a site
of this size; a CDN-cached single stylesheet would be the alternative at ten times the
page count.

---

## D-03 — One accent colour, no gradients

**Decision:** A single brand blue (`#115FC8`) on a paper/ink/mist palette. No gradients
anywhere, including decorative ones.

**Why:** A client requirement, and a good one: gradients are the fastest way for a
corporate site to look generic. Depth comes from tonal steps, hairlines and typography.

**Enforcement:** A computed-style sweep for `background-image` after each build.

---

## D-04 — Archivo + IBM Plex Mono

**Decision:** Archivo for display and body, Plex Mono for labels and metadata.

**Why:** Archivo is a neutral grotesque with a high x-height that holds up at 70px and at
14px, and it does not read as the default system stack. Plex Mono gives the technical
annotation layer its own voice without a third family.

**Rules:** three weights only (400 read, 500 emphasise, 600 announce); negative tracking
on display sizes; positive tracking on all caps.

---

## D-05 — The module lattice as the graphic language

**Decision:** Every diagram is built from the same square module at a 30px pitch: the
home system plate, the capability and product system maps, the engagement figures.

**Why:** The brand mark is a plus made of offset squares. Reusing that geometry makes the
graphics unmistakably Intactic's, and it avoids stock photography entirely — which is
also why there are no client logos or fabricated case-study images.

---

## D-06 — Tinted sections instead of white on white

**Decision:** A surface ladder — paper, mist, stone, ink — with a hard rule that no two
adjacent sections share a surface.

**Why:** Early screenshots showed long white stretches that read as unfinished. Tinting
the page head, the hero and the footer, and alternating the content bands, gives the page
structure without adding ornament. Cards stay white and therefore sit on a tint.

---

## D-07 — Fixed, opaque header

**Decision:** `position: fixed`, solid background, one hairline, no blur, on every device.

**Why:** Client requirement. Blur and translucency also fight the engineering aesthetic
and cost paint time on low-end phones.

**Consequence:** `body` carries `padding-top: 74px`; anchor scrolling uses
`scroll-padding-top` so headings are not hidden under the bar.

---

## D-08 — A dedicated page per capability and per product

**Decision:** Six capability pages and four product pages, each with its own copy and
diagram, rather than one long services page.

**Why:** The questions inside each discipline differ (payout ledgers vs offline sync vs
limitation periods). Separate pages let the writing be specific, give each discipline its
own URL for search, and let a reader stop at the one that matches their problem.

**Cost:** More copy to maintain, and a shared template that must stay flexible.

---

## D-09 — Copy rule: no AI-hype vocabulary

**Decision:** The site avoids "AI-first", "AI-powered", "cutting-edge", "seamless",
"leverage", "unlock", "transform", "next-gen" and similar. Where models are relevant, the
copy describes the mechanism (retrieval, review queue, evaluation set, fallback).

**Why:** A client requirement, and the differentiator: every competitor claims to be
AI-driven. Specific mechanism claims are believable; adjectives are not.

**Enforcement:** Automated sweep of visible text against a banned-word list.

---

## D-10 — Contact form posts through the visitor's mail client

**Decision:** The brief form composes a `mailto:` message with the fields pre-filled; it
does not post to a server.

**Why:** There is no backend yet, and a fake success message would be dishonest. The
button says "Prepare the brief", and the page states that the mail app will open.

**Follow-up:** Replace with a form endpoint when the site is deployed, keeping the same
field set and the same confirmation copy.

---

## D-11 — Documentation lives in the repository

**Decision:** `docs/` holds the project guide, design system, page inventory, decision
log, changelog and product facts. Every future change adds a changelog entry.

**Why:** A client requirement, and the only reliable way to hand a generated site to
another team: the generator, its rules and its history travel with the output.

---

## D-12 — Products as first-class pages, facts traced to source

**Decision:** Each product page states only what is evidenced by its repository or
stated by the owner. Repositories are not linked publicly (they are private); the product
domain is the public link.

**Why:** Invented product claims are a liability, and the repos are the source of truth.
`docs/PRODUCTS.md` records what was verified and what must not be claimed.

---

## D-13 — The site is a Next.js static export

**Decision:** The site is built by Next.js (`output: 'export'`) from TypeScript in
`next-app/src`; the publishable artefact is `next-app/out/`. **D-01 and D-02 are superseded.**

**Why:** D-01 chose plain generated HTML because a marketing site has no state to manage, and that
was right while the site was a dozen templates rendered from fragments. What changed is that ten of
the nineteen pages are now built from typed content, that changes are made by people who did not
write the generator, and that the site has a design system with rules to keep. The generator could
not make a mistyped icon name a compile error, and it kept the CSS outside the app it styled.

**What survives from D-02:** the requirement, not the mechanism. The export is still files on a
host; `next/font/local` self-hosts the same five faces and preloads them, so nothing comes from a
CDN and there is still no flash of fallback text. Base64 inlining is gone — it duplicated the fonts
into every page.

**Cost:** a framework and a build chain (Next 16, React 19, TypeScript) where there was a Python
script. Accepted because the gate now proves each change page by page instead of a person
re-reading nineteen files.

**Enforcement:** `npm run verify` — 19/19 routes, 0 errors, text parity at zero characters;
`qa:compare` — 114 screenshot pairs, 0 failures; `tsc --noEmit` — exit 0. The legacy generator
is kept in `legacy/` as content history and is not read by any build.

**Supersedes:** D-01 (static multi-page site generated from templates) · D-02 (everything inlined:
CSS, JS, fonts).

---

## D-14 — The brief form does not ask for a budget

**Decision:** The contact form asks for name, email, company, project type, timeline and a brief.
It does not ask for a budget range.

**Why:** In Bangladesh — the studio's home market — and on first contact anywhere, naming a budget
before the work is understood is not how the conversation starts. A public form that opens with
price brackets reads as a foreign template, and it costs the enquiry it was meant to qualify. The
price conversation belongs after a short discovery, when both sides know the shape of the work.

**What this settles:** the legacy form collected a "Budget range" that never reached the mailto
body — the one bug the port preserved on purpose. Removing the field resolves it by design instead
of leaving a control that does nothing.

**Not decided here:** whether to qualify on something else — team size, who signs off, deadline
pressure. If a qualifier is added later it goes into the form and the mailto builder together, so
the two cannot drift apart again.

**Enforced by:** `qa/reference/baseline.json` records the approved contact page after the removal,
with the reason in its `approvals` list; the gate fails if the page drifts back.

---

## D-15 — The admin panel is a local, build-time studio

**Decision:** The panel is a separate application (`admin-app/`) that runs on `127.0.0.1:3001`,
reads and writes `next-app/data/*.json`, and triggers the site's own build. It is never served from
the public artefact and has no auth, because it is not reachable from outside the machine.

**Why:** The site is a static export (D-13). A runtime CMS would need a server, a database, sessions
and a login — a second system to keep patched, and one that would either render the site dynamically
or write into the build anyway. The studio writes the source and lets the build judge it, so the
deployed artefact stays files in a folder and git stays the history of every change.

**Cost:** A build (about a minute) stands between a save and a live page, and the panel only works
where the repository is checked out. Both are acceptable for an owner-operated site; neither is
acceptable for a multi-author newsroom, which is not what this is.

**Scale-out path:** if the studio ever moves to the LAN or online, only the write layer behind the
API and the auth change; the UI, the forms and the build panel stay as they are.

**Enforced by:** `admin-app/` has its own `package.json` and never imports from `next-app/out/`;
the site's `npm run verify` contains no reference to the studio.

---

## D-16 — Content and configuration are JSON, validated in TypeScript

**Decision:** Capabilities, products, figures, the route manifest, the section registry and the site
configuration live in `next-app/data/*.json`. A runtime schema validates each file once, at import
time, and fails the build with the JSON path of the first problem.

**Why:** The studio must write these files, and TypeScript literals are not a format a program can
write safely. JSON is; the schema is what keeps the compile-time guarantee the literals had. Because
validation runs before a page is emitted, a typo is still a build failure rather than a blank section.

**Cost:** Two layers agree by hand — `types.ts` and `schema.ts` — and the studio keeps its own copy
of the shapes. The gate and the build validate both sides, which is what keeps that honest.

**Supersedes:** the typed literals introduced with the TypeScript port, not D-13.

---

## D-17 — The section registry is data, not code

**Decision:** Every section of every page is an entry in `next-app/data/sections.json`
(`page`, `id`, `title`, `kind`, `mount`, `locked`). `src/lib/sections.ts` validates it; the site
renders from it; the studio lists its controls from it.

**Why:** Both applications need the same list, and they cannot share a module: the studio is a
separate package, and importing the site's TypeScript would drag its bundle, its aliases and its
client boundary across the boundary the first decision draws. A JSON file both can read is the only
arrangement that keeps one source. It also makes the "new section, new control" promise literal: add
an entry, and the control appears.

**Guardrails:** the head (`head`/`hero`) and the closing CTA are `locked` on every route; the head
carries the h1 and the CTA is switched by the page's `showCta`, not by `hidden`. A section id in
`site-config.json` that the registry does not know fails the build, and so does a route without a
layout.

**Cost:** the section list is explicit rather than derived from a template, so the ten templated
pages carry their five body entries each. That is the price of a file a program can read and a human
can diff.
